paths.title: UI State, Rendering & Component Architecture
paths.description: Model state explicitly, derive views predictably, choose component boundaries, manage effects, and prevent inconsistent interface states.
topics: State versus derived data
State stores information that changes over time, while derived values can be computed from authoritative state and inputs.
Store the smallest authoritative state and compute totals, filtered lists, and labels instead of synchronizing duplicate copies.
State machines
Many interfaces have discrete states and allowed transitions that become clearer when modeled explicitly.
Represent loading, success, empty, error, editing, and confirmation transitions deliberately instead of combining unrelated booleans.
Single source of truth
Two independently mutable copies of the same information eventually diverge unless synchronization is perfect.
Choose one owner for each piece of state and pass values or events across boundaries rather than duplicating mutable state.
Component responsibility
A component boundary should encapsulate a coherent behavior, semantic region, or reusable UI contract.
Split components around stable responsibilities and data flow, not arbitrary line counts or every visual wrapper.
Inputs and outputs
Components become predictable when inputs are explicit and changes are communicated through narrow events or callbacks.
Define stable props/attributes and emitted events rather than reading or mutating distant global state implicitly.
Pure rendering
Rendering is easier to reason about when the same inputs produce the same output without hidden side effects.
Keep network calls, timers, subscriptions, and storage writes out of pure render calculations and place them in explicit lifecycle/effect boundaries.
Effect lifecycle
Effects synchronize UI with systems outside rendering and must account for setup, change, cancellation, and cleanup.
Tie subscriptions and requests to the state that requires them and clean them up when dependencies or component lifetime ends.
Optimistic UI
Optimistic updates improve responsiveness by showing the expected result before the server confirms it.
Use optimistic state only when rollback or reconciliation is defined and the server remains authoritative.
Local versus shared state
State should live as close as possible to the components that need it while genuinely shared state needs an explicit owner.
Start local, lift state to the nearest common owner when necessary, and introduce a global store only for cross-cutting shared domains.
Rendering identity
Stable keys and identity determine whether list items preserve component state or are recreated during updates.
Use durable data identifiers for keyed collections and never use changing random values as render keys.

paths.title: TypeScript, Modules & Frontend Tooling
paths.description: Use static types, module boundaries, package tooling, build systems, linting, formatting, source maps, and environment configuration responsibly.
topics: TypeScript purpose
TypeScript checks JavaScript-shaped programs before runtime but cannot validate arbitrary external data by itself.
Use types to model internal contracts and pair them with runtime validation at network, storage, or user-input boundaries.
Inference versus annotation
Type inference reduces redundant declarations while explicit annotations clarify public contracts and ambiguous values.
Let local values infer naturally and annotate exported APIs, callbacks, generics, and places where inference hides intent.
Narrowing
Type guards and control-flow analysis refine unions based on runtime checks.
Narrow unknown or union values before accessing members instead of suppressing errors with unsafe assertions.
Unknown versus any
unknown requires checking before use while any disables type safety and propagates unchecked assumptions.
Prefer unknown at untrusted boundaries and confine unavoidable any values behind small validated adapters.
Generics
Generics express relationships among types without discarding information into broad unions or any.
Use generics when callers preserve a type relationship, not merely to make simple functions look abstract.
Module boundaries
ES module imports and exports define the dependency graph used by browsers and build tools.
Keep modules cohesive, avoid circular dependencies, and expose a narrow public surface from each feature or package.
Package-lock reproducibility
Lockfiles capture resolved dependency versions so installs remain stable across machines and CI.
Commit the lockfile used by the package manager and use reproducible CI install commands rather than unconstrained updates.
Bundling and transforms
Build tools can bundle modules, transpile syntax, process assets, split chunks, and optimize production output.
Understand what the build actually transforms and avoid adding plugins for features the runtime already supports adequately.
Linting and formatting
Linters catch selected correctness or maintainability patterns while formatters standardize presentation.
Automate both in editor and CI, keep rules intentional, and avoid treating style compliance as proof of behavioral correctness.
Source maps and environments
Source maps map optimized code back to authored sources, while environment variables may be embedded into client bundles at build time.
Protect source-map access appropriately and never put server secrets into variables that frontend build tooling exposes to browser code.

paths.title: Frontend Accessibility Engineering
paths.description: Design for keyboard, screen readers, zoom, contrast, motion preferences, names and roles, focus, live updates, and WCAG-aligned verification.
topics: Native semantics first
Native HTML controls expose roles, states, keyboard behavior, and platform integration that custom widgets must recreate manually.
Choose the semantic element that already matches the interaction before adding ARIA or JavaScript behavior.
Keyboard operability
Every interactive function must be reachable and usable without a pointer, with a logical focus order.
Test all flows using Tab, Shift+Tab, Enter, Space, arrows where appropriate, and Escape for dismissible UI.
Visible focus
Keyboard users need a clear visual indication of the element that will receive input.
Use :focus-visible styles with sufficient contrast and never remove outlines without an equally clear replacement.
Accessible names
Controls need names exposed through text content, labels, aria-label, or aria-labelledby according to the element pattern.
Inspect the accessibility tree and verify that names describe the action or value without redundant role words.
Roles, states and properties
ARIA communicates semantics such as expanded, selected, pressed, invalid, current, or relationships when native HTML lacks them.
Update ARIA states at the same moment visible state changes and follow the interaction behavior defined for the pattern.
Color and contrast
Information cannot rely on color alone, and foreground/background pairs need sufficient contrast for the content and state.
Test text, icons, focus indicators, disabled distinctions, charts, and both light/dark themes with automated and manual checks.
Zoom and reflow
Users may zoom or enlarge text substantially, causing layouts that depend on fixed dimensions to clip or overlap.
Verify content at 200% zoom and larger text settings without loss of information or two-dimensional scrolling for normal content.
Dynamic announcements
Live regions can announce important asynchronous changes, but excessive announcements overwhelm screen-reader users.
Use status or aria-live for concise meaningful updates and avoid announcing every intermediate render.
Motion and vestibular safety
Large movement, parallax, and autoplaying animation can impair some users and distract others.
Respect reduced-motion preferences, provide controls for persistent motion, and keep essential understanding independent of animation.
Accessibility testing layers
Automated scanners catch only a subset of accessibility defects and cannot judge all semantics or interaction quality.
Combine linting/scanners with keyboard testing, accessibility-tree inspection, zoom/reflow checks, and representative screen-reader testing.
codeExamples: html

<button type="button" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="filters" id="filters-toggle">Filters</button>
<section id="filters" hidden aria-labelledby="filters-toggle">...</section>
css

:focus-visible { outline:3px solid CanvasText; outline-offset:3px; }
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) { .animated { animation:none; transition:none; } }

paths.title: Routing, Navigation & Complete UX States
paths.description: Design URLs, history, navigation, loading, empty, error, offline, permission, and recovery states as part of the product contract.
topics: URL as application state
Shareable application state belongs in durable URLs when users benefit from bookmarking, history, or deep links.
Represent route identity and stable filters in path/query parameters while keeping ephemeral UI state local.
History semantics
pushState adds a history entry while replaceState updates the current one; back/forward navigation must restore coherent UI.
Use push for meaningful navigation and replace for corrections or transient parameter changes that should not create extra Back presses.
Route ownership
Nested routes and layouts should have explicit ownership for data loading, errors, metadata, and navigation chrome.
Assign each route boundary a clear responsibility so child screens do not silently depend on global initialization side effects.
Navigation feedback
Route changes can involve network and rendering delays that need feedback without causing layout jumps.
Preserve stable chrome, show contextual pending indicators, and avoid blanking useful previous content unnecessarily.
Empty state
An empty result is often a legitimate domain state rather than an error.
Explain why no content exists and offer the most relevant next action, filter reset, or creation path.
Error state
Errors need enough context for users to recover while technical details belong in diagnostics rather than raw UI messages.
Differentiate retryable network failure, authorization, validation, not-found, and unexpected errors with appropriate recovery actions.
Offline state
Installed or resilient applications may need to function with cached content while disconnected.
Detect failed network-dependent operations, explain what remains available, and queue writes only when conflict semantics are defined.
Permission state
A user can be authenticated but lack permission for a route, object, or action.
Render authorization-aware UI without exposing forbidden data and let the server enforce every authoritative permission decision.
Unsaved changes
Navigation can destroy local edits when users leave a dirty form or multi-step task.
Track dirty state and warn only when data loss is real, while ensuring browser/session restoration does not create repeated prompts.
Focus and scroll after navigation
Client-side routing does not automatically reproduce all accessibility behaviors of full page navigation.
Update document title, move focus to meaningful route content, and define scroll restoration behavior after navigation.
codeExamples: javascript
javascript

window.addEventListener("popstate", () => renderRoute(location.pathname, location.search));
function navigate(url) { history.pushState(null, "", url); renderRoute(location.pathname, location.search); }

paths.title: Frontend Security & Privacy
paths.description: Reduce XSS, unsafe URL, third-party, storage, clickjacking, CSP, token, privacy, and supply-chain risks in browser applications.
topics: Cross-site scripting
XSS occurs when attacker-controlled content becomes executable script or markup in a trusted origin.
Prefer safe text/DOM APIs, contextual escaping, trusted templates, and vetted sanitization for intentionally allowed HTML.
Unsafe HTML sinks
innerHTML, outerHTML, insertAdjacentHTML, document.write, and similar sinks interpret strings as markup.
Keep untrusted data out of HTML-parsing sinks and centralize any required sanitization policy rather than scattering exceptions.
URL and navigation validation
javascript: URLs, open redirects, and untrusted target URLs can turn normal navigation features into attack surfaces.
Parse URLs, restrict allowed schemes/origins where required, and avoid copying arbitrary untrusted strings into navigation or resource attributes.
Content Security Policy
CSP restricts script and other resource execution sources and can reduce the impact of injection vulnerabilities.
Adopt nonce/hash-based script policies where feasible, monitor violations, and treat CSP as defense in depth rather than a replacement for safe rendering.
Token storage
Browser-accessible storage can be read by successful XSS, while cookies introduce their own CSRF and attribute considerations.
Choose authentication storage with the server architecture and threat model, using Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite cookies when cookie-based sessions fit.
CSRF awareness
Browsers automatically attach some credentials to cross-site requests, so state-changing endpoints may need CSRF defenses.
Use appropriate SameSite cookie settings and server-side CSRF protections; frontend code alone cannot enforce authoritative defense.
Third-party scripts
Analytics, widgets, tag managers, and external packages execute with significant access to page data and capabilities.
Minimize third-party code, pin or review dependencies, restrict capabilities, and load only integrations with clear business value.
Frame and opener risks
Embedding and window opener relationships can enable clickjacking, UI redress, or cross-window manipulation.
Use server frame-ancestors/X-Frame-Options policies and noopener behavior for untrusted new-window navigation.
Sensitive client data
Browser bundles, source maps, storage, logs, DOM attributes, and analytics are not appropriate places for secrets.
Assume users can inspect all shipped client data and minimize personal information retained or exposed in the browser.
Privacy by design
Tracking identifiers, fingerprinting, storage, and third-party requests create privacy implications beyond technical security.
Collect only necessary telemetry, document purposes and retention, respect consent requirements, and avoid sending sensitive values in URLs.
